events.title: Rider Advocate brief: 8 claims (0 void)
events.body:
C1: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 21:47–21:50 that added 1.73 km (1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, deviating up to 979 m), which is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route under RD-1. [F3 F1] [RD-1]
C2: No traffic incident near the route is recorded during the trip window (F13) and the only speed-band records are band 4 on the SLE and band 5 on the TPE (F11, F12) — neither is a band 1 or 2 record on the replaced optimal segment — so the driver has no RD-4 reasonable-cause exemption for the 1.73 km segment. [F13 F11 F12] [RD-4]
C3: The rider's consent in chat was limited to a one-minute petrol stop: the driver asked at 21:43 'Mind if I pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute?' (F7) and the rider replied at 21:44 merely 'Sure, no problem' (F8), naming no location and agreeing only to a brief stop, not to a 1.73 km loop. [F7 F8] [RD-5 RD-3]
C4: Because the rider never named a location, the driver unilaterally chose where to go and the chosen detour produced the off-route segment (F3), so under RD-3(b) the extra 1.73 km is not excused by the rider's 'stop for a moment' request; the stop time itself is charged via the meter and is not refunded. [F8 F3] [RD-3]
C5: This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (charged $40.18 metered, distance component $27.23 for 19.3 km at $1.41/km), so the metered excess enters the fare: the unexempted segment's extra 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44, which is the RD-2 partial refund, not the full $2.90 billed excess. [F6 F4 F3] [RD-2]
C6: The driver's post-trip statement that 'the rider agreed to a short stop so I thought a small change of route was fine' (F10) is not consent for the route change: it is a driver statement made after the trip, and the only rider message is F8, which names no location and does not cover the loop. [F10 F8] [RD-5]
C7: The charged amount is consistent with the actual GPS distance and time (F4, F6 vs F1, F2) with no surge and no waiting fee, so the only overcharge is the metered excess mileage attributable to the unexempted off-route segment; no ERP/toll item appears in the bill. [F4 F6 F5 F1] [RD-2 FARE-2]
C8: The driver's 90-day record shows 2 disputes, 2 upheld (F16), and a route_deviation finding against him here makes the conduct repeated, supporting the additional account-review action under RD-6. [F16] [RD-6]
Weaknesses: The rider did agree to a stop: F7 (driver's 21:43 request) and F8 (rider's 21:44 'Sure, no problem') predate the off-route segment start at 21:47, so the driver will argue RD-5/RD-3(a) consent covers the deviation; our answer is that the consent named no location and no distance, so it does not cover a 979 m-max deviation. | Part of the 2.1 km excess is not the segment: the off-route segment accounts for only 1.73 km of the 2.1 km total (F3 vs F1), so the 0.37 km residual (map-matching residue / other small deviation) is not refundable under RD-2 and we must not claim the full $2.90 (F4). | The driver's statement F10 is a plausible misreading of the consent rather than obvious bad faith, and the traffic record shows genuine moderate congestion on the SLE/TPE (F11, F12) at band 4–5, which the driver may use to paint the trip as slow rather than devious — though RD-4 does not accept bands 3–5 as a justification. | The rider's consent message gives the driver some scope to argue a petrol stop was reasonably 'just ahead' on his chosen route, so the exempted/uneaxmpted split depends on the judge reading F8 against F3.
Asks: refund_partial $2.44

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 21:47–21:50 that added 1.73 km (1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, deviating up to 979 m), which is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route under RD-1.

No traffic incident near the route is recorded during the trip window (F13) and the only speed-band records are band 4 on the SLE and band 5 on the TPE (F11, F12) — neither is a band 1 or 2 record on the replaced optimal segment — so the driver has no RD-4 reasonable-cause exemption for the 1.73 km segment.

The rider's consent in chat was limited to a one-minute petrol stop: the driver asked at 21:43 'Mind if I pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute?' (F7) and the rider replied at 21:44 merely 'Sure, no problem' (F8), naming no location and agreeing only to a brief stop, not to a 1.73 km loop.

Because the rider never named a location, the driver unilaterally chose where to go and the chosen detour produced the off-route segment (F3), so under RD-3(b) the extra 1.73 km is not excused by the rider's 'stop for a moment' request; the stop time itself is charged via the meter and is not refunded.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (charged $40.18 metered, distance component $27.23 for 19.3 km at $1.41/km), so the metered excess enters the fare: the unexempted segment's extra 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44, which is the RD-2 partial refund, not the full $2.90 billed excess.

The driver's post-trip statement that 'the rider agreed to a short stop so I thought a small change of route was fine' (F10) is not consent for the route change: it is a driver statement made after the trip, and the only rider message is F8, which names no location and does not cover the loop.

The charged amount is consistent with the actual GPS distance and time (F4, F6 vs F1, F2) with no surge and no waiting fee, so the only overcharge is the metered excess mileage attributable to the unexempted off-route segment; no ERP/toll item appears in the bill.
The driver's 90-day record shows 2 disputes, 2 upheld (F16), and a route_deviation finding against him here makes the conduct repeated, supporting the additional account-review action under RD-6.

weaknesses: The rider did agree to a stop: F7 (driver's 21:43 request) and F8 (rider's 21:44 'Sure, no problem') predate the off-route segment start at 21:47, so the driver will argue RD-5/RD-3(a) consent covers the deviation; our answer is that the consent named no location and no distance, so it does not cover a 979 m-max deviation.

Part of the 2.1 km excess is not the segment: the off-route segment accounts for only 1.73 km of the 2.1 km total (F3 vs F1), so the 0.37 km residual (map-matching residue / other small deviation) is not refundable under RD-2 and we must not claim the full $2.90 (F4).

The driver's statement F10 is a plausible misreading of the consent rather than obvious bad faith, and the traffic record shows genuine moderate congestion on the SLE/TPE (F11, F12) at band 4–5, which the driver may use to paint the trip as slow rather than devious — though RD-4 does not accept bands 3–5 as a justification.

The rider's consent message gives the driver some scope to argue a petrol stop was reasonably 'just ahead' on his chosen route, so the exempted/uneaxmpted split depends on the judge reading F8 against F3.

[F7 F8 F10] [RD-5]
D3: The excess billed as a result of the deviation is $2.90 (2.1 km at $1.41/km) on a $40.18 metered fare, so even on the claimant's best case the disputed sum is the excess-distance item only and there is no basis for disturbing the base fare of $3.90, the time charge of $7.58, or the platform fee of $1.47 (F4, F6) — and no surge applied (F5). [F4 F5 F6] [RD-2 FARE-1]
D4: There was no traffic incident near the route in the trip window (F13); the only ambient congestion recorded was on the Seletar Expressway (band 4, 30–39 km/h) and Tampines Expressway (band 5, 40–49 km/h) (F11, F12) in fair weather (F14) — so the deviation is not being excused as a forced reroute, it is defended solely as a rider-approved stop. [F11 F12 F13 F14] [RD-4]
D5: Neither party has a history of route disputes — the rider has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days and the driver's 2 upheld matters in 90 days are both no-show, not route (F15, F16) — so nothing in the profiles supports treating this isolated three-minute stop as repeated route misconduct; and no account flag is warranted on this record. [F15 F16] [RD-6]
Weaknesses: RD-3(b) cuts against us: the rider did not name a station, and the driver chose a point that created the off-route segment (up to 979 m from the optimal route), so the claimant will argue the consent covered 'a stop' and not this route change (F3, F7, F8). | RD-5 requires the consent message to precede the segment, and it does (21:44 vs 21:47 start) (F8, F3) — but the consent wording is generic ("Sure, no problem."), which lets the rider argue it did not reach this particular loop; the message must be read in his favour. | The rider's complaint that the driver never actually stopped for petrol is not contradicted by, and cannot be rebutted from, any GPS stop record in the fact table — only the fare facts show the meter, so we cannot prove a stop occurred. | The meter excess is real and computable: F4 ($2.90 for 2.1 km excess) and F6 (19.3 km actually billed), so if the judge is unpersuaded on consent an RD-2 refund is arithmetically ready at $2.90.

events.title: Rider Advocate rebuttal: 5 points
events.body:
→ D1: The timing of the consent is not in dispute (F8 at 21:44 precedes the segment start at 21:47 in F3), but timing alone does not satisfy RD-5: the consent must cover the segment, and the rider's message named no location while the driver's question asked only to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' (F7), so the change of route to a point up to 979 m off the optimal route is outside what was agreed. [F7 F8 F3] [RD-5]
→ D2: RD-3(b) governs exactly this situation: the rider did not name a place, the driver chose the point that produced the off-route segment, and the rider agreed only to 'a stop', not to that route change — so the 1.73 km extra_km is not exempted by the chat. The driver's own statement F10 is a post-trip claim about what he thought the agreement covered and cannot expand the scope of F8. [F8 F3 F10 F7] [RD-3 RD-5]
→ D3: We do not ask to disturb base, time, platform fee or surge; the refund is confined to the metered mileage of the unexempted segment, computed under RD-2 as 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44 (F3, F6), not the full $2.90 billed excess (F4) which includes the 0.37 km non-segment residual. [F3 F6 F4] [RD-2]
→ D4: The driver's own position that the deviation was a rider-approved stop leaves the segment with no RD-4 exemption at all: the traffic records show only band 4 and band 5 on the SLE and TPE (F11, F12), not band 1 or 2 on the replaced optimal route, and no incident (F13), so RD-4(c) sends the segment back to RD-2. [F11 F12 F13] [RD-4]
→ D5: RD-6 only requires that the rider win this case and that the driver have at least one upheld dispute in the last 90 days, which F16 shows (2 disputes, 2 upheld), and the profile window does not exempt no-show matters — so the flag is an available additional action, and in any event it does not change the $2.44 refund we seek. [F16] [RD-6]
Revised ask: refund_partial $2.44

points.response: The timing of the consent is not in dispute (F8 at 21:44 precedes the segment start at 21:47 in F3), but timing alone does not satisfy RD-5: the consent must cover the segment, and the rider's message named no location while the driver's question asked only to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' (F7), so the change of route to a point up to 979 m off the optimal route is outside what was agreed.

RD-3(b) governs exactly this situation: the rider did not name a place, the driver chose the point that produced the off-route segment, and the rider agreed only to 'a stop', not to that route change — so the 1.73 km extra_km is not exempted by the chat. The driver's own statement F10 is a post-trip claim about what he thought the agreement covered and cannot expand the scope of F8.

We do not ask to disturb base, time, platform fee or surge; the refund is confined to the metered mileage of the unexempted segment, computed under RD-2 as 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44 (F3, F6), not the full $2.90 billed excess (F4) which includes the 0.37 km non-segment residual.

events.title: Driver Advocate rebuttal: 7 points
events.body:
→ C1: The claim that the segment is 'unexplained' ignores the record: the deviation the rider complains of is exactly the segment the rider was told about at 21:43 and agreed to at 21:44 (F7, F8), which is the explanation RD-1/RD-5 require, and the remaining 0.37 km of the 2.1 km total is map-matching residue on a 17.3 km trip, not a separate deviation (F1, F3). [F1 F3 F7 F8] [RD-1 RD-5]
→ C2 (concedes): Conceded only in the narrow sense: we do not claim an RD-4 traffic exemption, because none is needed — F11 and F12 show ordinary moderate congestion and F13 shows no incident, and the ground of defence is the rider's own pre-segment consent under RD-5, not reasonable cause under RD-4 (F7, F8, F11, F12, F13). [F7 F8 F11 F12 F13] [RD-4 RD-5]
→ C3: The message F7 the rider agreed to reads 'the petrol station just ahead', a specific place identified by the driver and accepted by the rider, and F8's 'Sure, no problem' is an unqualified assent to that stated place, not to an abstract 'stop' (F7, F8). [F7 F8] [RD-5 RD-3]
→ C4: RD-3(b) applies only where the driver '事前未告知乘客该地点' (did not tell the rider the place in advance); here the driver told the rider the place — the petrol station just ahead — at 21:43, three minutes before the segment began at 21:47, and the rider said 'Sure, no problem.' (F7, F8, F3). [F3 F7 F8] [RD-3 RD-5]
→ C5: We accept that on a RydeTAXI trip any unexempted segment's extra km would enter the meter at $1.41/km, but there is no unexempted segment: the agreed petrol stop is exempt, so the RD-2 computation yields zero and no refund item arises (F3, F4, F6). [F3 F4 F6] [RD-2]
→ C6: F10 is not the basis of the consent — the basis is F8 itself, a rider-sent message timestamped 21:44, three minutes before the off-route segment started at 21:47, which is exactly the 'before you go' sequence RD-5 requires (F8, F3, F10). [F3 F8 F10] [RD-5]
→ C8: F16 shows both upheld matters in the last 90 days are no-show cases, not route cases, so this dispute would not be a repeated route violation, and using a profile fact as the main ground is barred because profiles may never decide the case (F16). [F15 F16] [RD-6]

Conceded only in the narrow sense: we do not claim an RD-4 traffic exemption, because none is needed — F11 and F12 show ordinary moderate congestion and F13 shows no incident, and the ground of defence is the rider's own pre-segment consent under RD-5, not reasonable cause under RD-4 (F7, F8, F11, F12, F13).

The message F7 the rider agreed to reads 'the petrol station just ahead', a specific place identified by the driver and accepted by the rider, and F8's 'Sure, no problem' is an unqualified assent to that stated place, not to an abstract 'stop' (F7, F8).

RD-3(b) applies only where the driver '事前未告知乘客该地点' (did not tell the rider the place in advance); here the driver told the rider the place — the petrol station just ahead — at 21:43, three minutes before the segment began at 21:47, and the rider said 'Sure, no problem.' (F7, F8, F3).

We accept that on a RydeTAXI trip any unexempted segment's extra km would enter the meter at $1.41/km, but there is no unexempted segment: the agreed petrol stop is exempt, so the RD-2 computation yields zero and no refund item arises (F3, F4, F6).

F10 is not the basis of the consent — the basis is F8 itself, a rider-sent message timestamped 21:44, three minutes before the off-route segment started at 21:47, which is exactly the 'before you go' sequence RD-5 requires (F8, F3, F10).

F16 shows both upheld matters in the last 90 days are no-show cases, not route cases, so this dispute would not be a repeated route violation, and using a profile fact as the main ground is barred because profiles may never decide the case (F16).

what_would_change: F3: if the judge finds the rider agreed to this route or named this stop beforehand, it is exempt; if not, $2.44 is refunded; if the record cannot settle it, a person decides.
Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 21:47–21:50 that added 1.73 km (1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, deviating up to 979 m), which is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route under RD-1.

No traffic incident near the route is recorded during the trip window (F13) and the only speed-band records are band 4 on the SLE and band 5 on the TPE (F11, F12) — neither is a band 1 or 2 record on the replaced optimal segment — so the driver has no RD-4 reasonable-cause exemption for the 1.73 km segment.

The rider's consent in chat was limited to a one-minute petrol stop: the driver asked at 21:43 'Mind if I pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute?' (F7) and the rider replied at 21:44 merely 'Sure, no problem' (F8), naming no location and agreeing only to a brief stop, not to a 1.73 km loop.

Because the rider never named a location, the driver unilaterally chose where to go and the chosen detour produced the off-route segment (F3), so under RD-3(b) the extra 1.73 km is not excused by the rider's 'stop for a moment' request; the stop time itself is charged via the meter and is not refunded.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (charged $40.18 metered, distance component $27.23 for 19.3 km at $1.41/km), so the metered excess enters the fare: the unexempted segment's extra 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44, which is the RD-2 partial refund, not the full $2.90 billed excess.

The driver's post-trip statement that 'the rider agreed to a short stop so I thought a small change of route was fine' (F10) is not consent for the route change: it is a driver statement made after the trip, and the only rider message is F8, which names no location and does not cover the loop.

The charged amount is consistent with the actual GPS distance and time (F4, F6 vs F1, F2) with no surge and no waiting fee, so the only overcharge is the metered excess mileage attributable to the unexempted off-route segment; no ERP/toll item appears in the bill.
The driver's 90-day record shows 2 disputes, 2 upheld (F16), and a route_deviation finding against him here makes the conduct repeated, supporting the additional account-review action under RD-6.

weaknesses: The rider did agree to a stop: F7 (driver's 21:43 request) and F8 (rider's 21:44 'Sure, no problem') predate the off-route segment start at 21:47, so the driver will argue RD-5/RD-3(a) consent covers the deviation; our answer is that the consent named no location and no distance, so it does not cover a 979 m-max deviation.

Part of the 2.1 km excess is not the segment: the off-route segment accounts for only 1.73 km of the 2.1 km total (F3 vs F1), so the 0.37 km residual (map-matching residue / other small deviation) is not refundable under RD-2 and we must not claim the full $2.90 (F4).

The driver's statement F10 is a plausible misreading of the consent rather than obvious bad faith, and the traffic record shows genuine moderate congestion on the SLE/TPE (F11, F12) at band 4–5, which the driver may use to paint the trip as slow rather than devious — though RD-4 does not accept bands 3–5 as a justification.

The rider's consent message gives the driver some scope to argue a petrol stop was reasonably 'just ahead' on his chosen route, so the exempted/uneaxmpted split depends on the judge reading F8 against F3.

claims.assertion: The only recorded off-route segment is a short 3-minute, 1.73-km deviation at 21:47–21:50 (F3), which the rider knew about and agreed to before it began: the driver asked at 21:43 and the rider replied "Sure, no problem." at 21:44 (F7, F8), both timestamps preceding the segment start at 21:47; on the face of the message the rider consented to a stop for petrol — a stop the driver plainly needed, since the driver said the tank was almost empty (F7).

The rider's complaint is that he agreed to a stop but the driver "never stopped for petrol anyway"; the rider agreed to the purpose of the stop rather than to a specific named place, and the driver's written statement that the rider agreed to a short stop is consistent with the chat exchange (F8, F10) — so the deviation was made with the rider's knowledge and for the reason the rider accepted, i.e. the change of route was not made without permission.

The excess billed as a result of the deviation is $2.90 (2.1 km at $1.41/km) on a $40.18 metered fare, so even on the claimant's best case the disputed sum is the excess-distance item only and there is no basis for disturbing the base fare of $3.90, the time charge of $7.58, or the platform fee of $1.47 (F4, F6) — and no surge applied (F5).

There was no traffic incident near the route in the trip window (F13); the only ambient congestion recorded was on the Seletar Expressway (band 4, 30–39 km/h) and Tampines Expressway (band 5, 40–49 km/h) (F11, F12) in fair weather (F14) — so the deviation is not being excused as a forced reroute, it is defended solely as a rider-approved stop.

Neither party has a history of route disputes — the rider has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days and the driver's 2 upheld matters in 90 days are both no-show, not route (F15, F16) — so nothing in the profiles supports treating this isolated three-minute stop as repeated route misconduct; and no account flag is warranted on this record.

weaknesses: RD-3(b) cuts against us: the rider did not name a station, and the driver chose a point that created the off-route segment (up to 979 m from the optimal route), so the claimant will argue the consent covered 'a stop' and not this route change (F3, F7, F8).

RD-5 requires the consent message to precede the segment, and it does (21:44 vs 21:47 start) (F8, F3) — but the consent wording is generic ("Sure, no problem."), which lets the rider argue it did not reach this particular loop; the message must be read in his favour.

The rider's complaint that the driver never actually stopped for petrol is not contradicted by, and cannot be rebutted from, any GPS stop record in the fact table — only the fare facts show the meter, so we cannot prove a stop occurred.
The meter excess is real and computable: F4 ($2.90 for 2.1 km excess) and F6 (19.3 km actually billed), so if the judge is unpersuaded on consent an RD-2 refund is arithmetically ready at $2.90.

points.response: The timing of the consent is not in dispute (F8 at 21:44 precedes the segment start at 21:47 in F3), but timing alone does not satisfy RD-5: the consent must cover the segment, and the rider's message named no location while the driver's question asked only to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' (F7), so the change of route to a point up to 979 m off the optimal route is outside what was agreed.

RD-3(b) governs exactly this situation: the rider did not name a place, the driver chose the point that produced the off-route segment, and the rider agreed only to 'a stop', not to that route change — so the 1.73 km extra_km is not exempted by the chat. The driver's own statement F10 is a post-trip claim about what he thought the agreement covered and cannot expand the scope of F8.

We do not ask to disturb base, time, platform fee or surge; the refund is confined to the metered mileage of the unexempted segment, computed under RD-2 as 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44 (F3, F6), not the full $2.90 billed excess (F4) which includes the 0.37 km non-segment residual.

The driver's own position that the deviation was a rider-approved stop leaves the segment with no RD-4 exemption at all: the traffic records show only band 4 and band 5 on the SLE and TPE (F11, F12), not band 1 or 2 on the replaced optimal route, and no incident (F13), so RD-4(c) sends the segment back to RD-2.

RD-6 only requires that the rider win this case and that the driver have at least one upheld dispute in the last 90 days, which F16 shows (2 disputes, 2 upheld), and the profile window does not exempt no-show matters — so the flag is an available additional action, and in any event it does not change the $2.44 refund we seek.

The claim that the segment is 'unexplained' ignores the record: the deviation the rider complains of is exactly the segment the rider was told about at 21:43 and agreed to at 21:44 (F7, F8), which is the explanation RD-1/RD-5 require, and the remaining 0.37 km of the 2.1 km total is map-matching residue on a 17.3 km trip, not a separate deviation (F1, F3).

Conceded only in the narrow sense: we do not claim an RD-4 traffic exemption, because none is needed — F11 and F12 show ordinary moderate congestion and F13 shows no incident, and the ground of defence is the rider's own pre-segment consent under RD-5, not reasonable cause under RD-4 (F7, F8, F11, F12, F13).

The message F7 the rider agreed to reads 'the petrol station just ahead', a specific place identified by the driver and accepted by the rider, and F8's 'Sure, no problem' is an unqualified assent to that stated place, not to an abstract 'stop' (F7, F8).

RD-3(b) applies only where the driver '事前未告知乘客该地点' (did not tell the rider the place in advance); here the driver told the rider the place — the petrol station just ahead — at 21:43, three minutes before the segment began at 21:47, and the rider said 'Sure, no problem.' (F7, F8, F3).

We accept that on a RydeTAXI trip any unexempted segment's extra km would enter the meter at $1.41/km, but there is no unexempted segment: the agreed petrol stop is exempt, so the RD-2 computation yields zero and no refund item arises (F3, F4, F6).

F10 is not the basis of the consent — the basis is F8 itself, a rider-sent message timestamped 21:44, three minutes before the off-route segment started at 21:47, which is exactly the 'before you go' sequence RD-5 requires (F8, F3, F10).

F16 shows both upheld matters in the last 90 days are no-show cases, not route cases, so this dispute would not be a repeated route violation, and using a profile fact as the main ground is barred because profiles may never decide the case (F16).

notices.text:
We reviewed your fare dispute. We found one part of the trip where the driver left the best route: 1.73 km between 21:47 and 21:50. Nothing in the trip record excuses that stretch, so we are refunding it.

You'll get $2.44 as a Ryde voucher. The rest of the fare, including the base, time and platform fee, stays as charged.

Your account stays in good standing and no action is needed from you.

We reviewed a fare dispute on this trip and found one off-route stretch: 1.73 km between 21:47 and 21:50. Your message mentioned stopping at a petrol station, but a named stop does not cover the driving distance used to reach it, and the rider did not agree to that extra leg. So that part of the fare is not upheld.

We are refunding $2.44 to the rider as a Ryde voucher. This route breach is noted on your file — no account flag, and no other action is needed from you.
